 Amendments NS-EN 1995-1-1:2004/A1:2008 and NS-EN 1995-1-1:2004/A2:2014 as well as corrigendum NS-EN 1995-1-1:2004/AC:2006 are incorporated in the Norwegian translation but are not incorporated in the text of the English version.  The standard assumes the use of a number of parameters to be determined nationally, denoted Nationally Determined Parameters or NDP, given in a National Annex to the standard, NA. The standard can only be used for the design of load-bearing structures together with the nationally determined parameters applicable in the country where a structure or a product is to be used. The standard, therefore, can only be used as a basis for design of structures or products to be used in Norway together with the requirements given in the Norwegian national annex to the standard. The standard specifies recommended values for the nationally determined parameters, these can not be used as replacement for the nationally determined parameters.
 National Annexes are in principle informative. According to §10-2 in the Technical Regulations to the Planning and Building Act (pbl) the essential requirements to mechanical resistance and stability, including geotechnichs, may be met by design of structures in accordance with Norwegian Standard NS- EN 1990 Eurocode: Basis of structural design and underlying standards in the series NS-EN 1991 to NS- EN 1999, with their National Annexes. Consequently the National Annexes will in practice have to be considered as normative.

 NS-EN 1995-1-1 is part of the series of Eurocodes. The standards in the Eurocode series are regarded as a consistant set of design rules, thus they should not be used together with the design standards in the series of NS 34XX. In March 2010 the design standards in the NS34XX-series was withdrawn. From then only the Eurocodes apply.

 In 1975, the Commission of the European Community decided on an action programme in the field of construction, based on article 95 of the Treaty. The objective of the programme was the elimination of technical obstacles to trade and the harmonisation of technical specifications.
 Within this action programme, the Commission took the initiative to establish a set of harmonised technical rules for the design of construction works which, in a first stage, would serve as an alternative to the national rules in force in the Member States and, ultimately, would replace them.
 For fifteen years, the Commission, with the help of a Steering Committee with Representatives of Member States, conducted the development of the Eurocodes programme, which led to the first generation of European codes in the 1980s.
 In 1989, the Commission and the Member States of the EU and EFTA decided, on the basis of an agreementT 1 T between the Commission and CEN, to transfer the preparation and the publication of the Eurocodes to CEN through a series of Mandates, in order to provide them with a future status of European Standard (EN). This links de facto the Eurocodes with the provisions of all the Council’s Directives and/or Commission’s Decisions dealing with European standards (e.g. the Council Directive 89/106/EEC on construction products – CPD – and Council Directives 93/37/EEC, 92/50/EEC and 89/440/EEC on public works and services and equivalent EFTA Directives initiated in pursuit of setting up the internal market).
